Text.name: scope_rule_text
Text.value: General rule: first decide whether the camera room has a unique and reproducible enclosed boundary. If it cannot be closed without guessing, choose the best OOS reason. Even for OOS cases, complete any required geometry fields and use Scope as the authoritative OOS signal.

Choices.name: scope
Choices.requiredMessage: Scope is required. Select exactly one option.

Choice.hint: Include only the room where the camera is located. Do not cross doorways or extend into adjacent rooms. Choose this when the current camera room still has a unique and reproducible wall-ceiling-floor enclosure. Stairs, openings, or ceiling recesses are not automatically OOS if you can stop at a clear room boundary.

Use when the current camera room itself cannot be stably represented by a single Manhattan/cuboid-style enclosure. Typical cases include curved walls, continuous curved surfaces, obvious slanted walls, or a dominant non-Manhattan room structure.

Choice.value: OOS: open or ambiguous camera-room boundary
Choice.hint: Use when the space is visible but the camera room cannot be closed at a reproducible boundary. Typical cases include missing door frames, missing wall stops, ambiguous turns, or multiple equally plausible closures. If the main problem is missing or invisible evidence, prefer insufficient evidence.

Use when the main room enclosure no longer satisfies a single-floor and single-ceiling assumption. Typical cases include stair bottoms, sunken areas, multi-level floors, or split ceilings directly entering the main enclosure. If the level change can be cleanly excluded at a boundary and the main enclosure remains unique, choose in-scope.

Use when key geometric evidence is missing and a reproducible enclosure cannot be determined. Typical causes include severe occlusion, overexposure, blur, missing panorama regions, black borders, or masks. Do not use this for minor local occlusions when the main enclosure is still stable.

Text.name: difficulty_rule_text
Text.value: Rule: select the difficulty factors that actually make corner annotation harder, not every visual issue in the image. Select at least one option. If you choose "trivial", do not select any other difficulty label; if any real difficulty exists, do not choose trivial.

Choices.name: difficulty
Choices.requiredMessage: Difficulty is required. Select at least one option.

Choice.hint: The scene is simple, geometry is clear, and there is no meaningful occlusion or distortion. Corner annotation should be almost effortless.

Important geometric evidence is locally blocked. Furniture, doors, wall partitions, foreground structures, or similar objects may occlude corners or boundaries. Choose this when the main enclosure is still reproducibly closed despite local blockage.

Local texture or color contrast is weak, so boundaries or corners rely mainly on subtle geometric cues rather than clear appearance changes. Do not choose this if the main difficulty is occlusion, seam/stretch, reflection, or low image quality.

Panorama stitching, reprojection, stretching, or local geometric distortion makes true corners hard to locate. This may appear as broken lines, shifted walls, or corner drift; the root cause is seam/stretch distortion.
Mirrors, glass, or reflective surfaces create false boundaries or visually confusing room structure.

Choice.value: Blur, mask, or low image quality
Choice.hint: Blur, noise, compression artifacts, large masks, black borders, or missing areas make key wall-floor-ceiling evidence unreliable. Prefer occlusion or seam/stretch when the problem is only local and more specific.

Text.name: model_issue_rule_text
Text.value: Rule: select at least one model-issue label. Choose "acceptable" only when the proposal is mostly reasonable and needs no major correction. If any issue exists, do not choose acceptable.

Choices.name: model_issue
Choices.requiredMessage: Model Issue is required. Select at least one option.

Choice.hint: The proposal is high quality and needs no major correction, or only minor adjustment.

The model includes a doorway/opening and extends into an adjacent space as if it were part of the same camera room. A human can usually correct this by stopping at the door frame, wall stop, or room boundary.
The model covers only part of the camera room and misses visible walls, corners, or boundaries.

The model treats cabinets, wall bumps, furniture edges, decorative protrusions, or other non-layout details as real layout corners or boundaries. If the main issue is multiple points around the same physical corner, prefer duplicate corner points.

One or a few corners or local boundaries are near the correct location but do not land exactly on the true wall corner. The topology is mostly correct and can usually be fixed by small dragging adjustments.
The same physical corner is represented by multiple nearby points. Delete redundant points and keep the one best supported by geometry.

Ceiling/floor points cannot be paired, the layout does not close, self-intersections appear, or another invalid topology occurs. If the whole proposal is essentially unusable, prefer prediction failure.

The initialization is globally misleading and must almost be redrawn from scratch. Use this only when the error is not better described by over-extension, under-extension, over-parsing, drift, duplicate points, or topology failure.
